config.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

intro.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
intro.body: In this lesson, you will implement an algorithm to find the maximum possible profit from a single buy and sell transaction given a list of daily stock prices. The core concept you will learn is how to efficiently track the minimum price seen so far and calculate the maximum profit in a single pass through the data. You will use fundamental JavaScript constructs like loops, variables, and conditional logic to build the solution. This exercise introduces you to a common pattern for solving optimization lessons with arrays, helping you think about time and space efficiency.
intro.usecase: The 'Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock' algorithm is fundamental to financial technology applications, particularly in trading platforms and investment dashboards. Developers implement this pattern in stock analysis tools to calculate maximum potential profit from historical price data, helping investors identify optimal buy/sell points. You'll see this in portfolio management interfaces where profit/loss calculations are displayed alongside price charts, and in algorithmic trading systems that automatically execute trades based on profit-maximization logic. Understanding this algorithm is essential for building financial applications that analyze market data and provide actionable investment insights.

objectives: Implement a brute force solution to find the maximum profit from stock prices
Construct an optimized solution using a single pass through the price array
Initialize and update variables to track minimum price and maximum profit
Manipulate array indices to compare buying and selling days
Apply the algorithm to solve the lesson with O(n) time complexity
Integrate the solution into a function that accepts an array of prices
Control loop iterations to prevent selling before buying

content.body: Welcome! Today we'll solve a classic lesson: finding the best time to buy and sell a stock to maximize profit. You'll learn how to track the lowest price seen so far and calculate potential profit in one pass through the prices array.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain why tracking the minimum price is key to finding maximum profit.
2. Implement a single-pass solution using a variable to remember the lowest price seen.
3. Calculate profit by comparing current price with the minimum seen so far.
4. Return the maximum possible profit from a series of daily prices.
5. Recognize when to update the minimum price versus when to calculate profit.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Given prices [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4], what's the maximum profit you could make by buying low and selling high?
content.successMessage: Great! You found that buying at 1 and selling at 6 gives a profit of 5.

content.title: Try a different array
content.prompt: Now try [3, 8, 1, 4, 7, 2]. What's the maximum profit?
content.successMessage: Excellent! Buying at 3 and selling at 8 gives profit 5, or buying at 1 and selling at 7 gives profit 6. The maximum is 6.

content.title: One more challenge
content.prompt: What about [9, 7, 5, 3, 2, 1]? Can you make any profit?
content.successMessage: Right! When prices only go down, the best profit is 0 (don't buy at all).

content.body: You just did a manual scan: you looked for the lowest price to buy, then the highest price after that to sell. For small arrays, you can visually spot the pattern, but for thousands of prices, we need a systematic approach.
content.title: What you did

content.body: With 10,000 daily prices, checking every possible buy-sell pair would be incredibly slow. We need a method that finds the answer in one pass through the data. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. As we move through the prices, we can keep track of the lowest price we've encountered so far. Then, for each new price, we check: if we bought at that lowest price and sold now, what profit would we make?
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where you write down the cheapest price you've seen so far. At each new day, you check if selling today would beat your best profit, and update your notebook if today's price is even lower.

content.body: We'll use a single variable to remember the minimum price seen so far, and another to track maximum profit. As we iterate through prices, we update both when needed.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with [7,1,5,3,6,4]:
Start: minPrice = Infinity, maxProfit = 0
Price 7: minPrice = 7, profit = 0
Price 1: minPrice = 1 (update), profit = 0
Price 5: profit = 4, maxProfit = 4
Price 3: profit = 2, maxProfit stays 4
Price 6: profit = 5, maxProfit = 5
Price 4: profit = 3, maxProfit stays 5
Result: 5

content.body:
1. Initialize minPrice to a very high value (or first price)
2. Initialize maxProfit to 0
3. For each price in the array:
   a. Calculate potential profit = price - minPrice
   b. Update maxProfit if profit is greater
   c. Update minPrice if current price is lower
4. Return maxProfit
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called maxProfit that takes a prices array as parameter.
steps.hint: Use function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure you include the prices parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function that accepts the prices array.

steps.title: Initialize tracking variables
steps.instruction: Inside the function, initialize minPrice to Infinity and maxProfit to 0.
steps.hint: Use let or const to declare variables.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! Check that you've set minPrice to Infinity and maxProfit to 0.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: we need minPrice to start very high, and maxProfit starts at 0.

steps.title: Loop through prices
steps.instruction: Add a for loop to iterate through each price in the prices array.
steps.hint: Use for...of or traditional for loop.
steps.expectedOutcome: Loop structure that accesses each price
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now we can process each price one by one.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there! Make sure your loop goes through all elements of prices.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to iterate through the entire prices array. Try a for loop.

steps.title: Implement the logic
steps.instruction: Inside the loop: 1) Update maxProfit if current price - minPrice is greater, 2) Update minPrice if current price is lower.
steps.hint: Use if statements to compare values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're both calculating profit and updating minPrice when needed.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: we need to check profit first, then update minPrice if this price is lower.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented an efficient O(n) solution to the stock profit lesson. Remember: the key insight is to track the minimum price seen so far as you iterate. This 'remember what we've seen' pattern is powerful for many array lessons. Try testing your function with different price arrays to see it in action!
content.title: Done
